Reading · quiet people

1.1 Discuss. In a meeting or a class, do you speak first or wait? Does the person who speaks most usually have the best idea?

KEY WORDS

reckless dangerous and careless

regardless of no matter what

open-plan with no separate rooms

perceptive quick to notice and understand

Why the World Needs Introverts

A few years ago I sat in a meeting where the loudest person in the room won an argument he was clearly wrong about. Nobody disagreed with him, because he had spoken first, spoken longest and spoken with complete confidence. Afterwards, three people told me privately that they had thought the idea was terrible. Not one of them had said so at the time.

We tend to treat confidence as evidence of ability, although the two have almost nothing to do with each other. Studies of group decision-making find that the person who talks most is seen as the leader, regardless of the quality of what they actually say. In schools, the quiet child is described as shy; the noisy one is described as a natural leader.

Susan Cain, who wrote a well-known book on the subject, argues that this costs organisations a great deal of money. Introverts think before they speak, listen more carefully and are far less likely to take reckless risks. A workplace built entirely around meetings, open-plan offices and group brainstorming quietly wastes about a third of its people.

None of this means that introverts are better. The point is narrower and more practical: the best idea in a room is not always the loudest one, and a good manager finds a way to hear the rest. Sometimes that is as simple as asking everyone to write their thoughts down before anybody speaks.

Grammar · articles

PRESENTATION

a / an — one of many, mentioned for the first time; also jobs and descriptions:

I met a manager yesterday. · She's an engineer. · It was a difficult meeting.

the — the listener knows which one: second mention, unique things, superlatives, of-phrases:

The manager I met was rude. · the sun · the best idea · the top of the page

no article (–) — plural and uncountable nouns used generally; most names:

– Introverts think before they speak. · – Confidence is not the same as – ability.

a / an — one of many, first mention

the — we both know which one

I work with an engineer.

The engineer I work with is Polish.

She wants a quiet office.

The office was far too noisy.

He's a good manager.

He's the best manager we've had.

There's a meeting today.

The meeting starts at nine.

ERROR WARNING

A singular countable noun always needs an article or another determiner:

She is teacher. ✗ She is a teacher. ✓

Do not use the with a general idea:

The life is hard. ✗ Life is hard. ✓ · The most of people ✗ Most people ✓

Institutions: go to – school / – bed / – work / – hospital (for the purpose) · go to the school (the building).

VOCABULARY NOTE

English speakers usually soften a negative judgement about a person:

He can be a bit difficult. · She's rather stubborn. · He tends to interrupt.

He comes across as slightly arrogant is far more natural than He is arrogant. · quite good = fairly good, but quite brilliant = completely brilliant.

Everyday English · describing people diplomatically

4.1 Read the conversation.

Malika What's the new team leader like?

Sardor Hard to say yet. She comes across as quite reserved.

Malika Reserved as in shy, or reserved as in unfriendly?

Sardor Shy, I think. She tends to listen before she says anything.

Malika That's a change. The last one could be a bit bossy.

Sardor A bit? He was impossible.

Malika Well — let's give her a month.

Asking about people

Describing carefully

Agreeing / disagreeing

What's she like?

She comes across as…

That's true, actually.

What's he like as a manager?

He can be a bit…

Do you think so? I'd say…

How do you find her?

She tends to…

Exactly. / Not at all.

ERROR WARNING

What is she like? = describe her. What does she like? = her preferences.

How is she like? ✗ What is she like? ✓

Writing · an informal online advert

5.1 Write an online advert (120–150 words): a room to rent, a language partner or something to sell.

PLAN

Headline — short and clear: Bright double room in quiet flat — free from 1 September

Details — what, where, how much, when. The person you want — Looking for someone tidy and easy-going.

Language of adverts: words are often left out. (There is) a bright room available. → Bright room available.

Keep the articles in your full sentences, but drop them in the headline and the list of details.
